Title: 2024: The movie watchlist year
body:
In 2024, I started replacing my "New year's resolutions" with "The year's goals" instead. Not to stop resolutions and building better habits, but more so to stop stressing over a lack of overnight metamorphosis, where I'm anxious about why am I not **x** already at month number **y**? So if the resolution for 2024 was *to be more mindful and appreciate media, mainly films, more deeply again*, I ended up planning a 12 month plan with at least one movie from my ever-growing watchlist a month, and to earnestly write a thought-out and honest critique of the movie, afterwards.

I ended up watching over 30 films throughout the year, with 12 I'm counting as part of the goal per my arbitrary conditions, i.e., I must have already have it on my watchlist before starting this goal **AND** must have been released in 2022 or earlier. For all of the movies, I can honestly say I enjoyed the actual act of watching more than I used to prior to setting this year's goals. I was a more active watcher in the sense I was noticing more of the directorial decisions, subtle acting choices, and especially on the specific things that I liked and not liked about a movie.

A full list of the aforementioned 12 movies from my watchlist will be at the table below but first, I want to highlight some notable ones to me:

• I started the year off with Ryusuke Hamaguchi's Drive my Car, the Best International Feature in 2021, and a Best picture, nominee that gave off uneasiness and an overwhelming ambiance further amplified by the ~3 hours of movie length and **my** lack of Japanese language skills, but this feeling coming, settling, and going also paralleled with Yusuke's and Misaki's understanding of each other in the film;

• Orson Welles' Citizen Kane was a pleasant surprise in that I was actively watching the film without getting distracted from the amount of things I've learned *about* the film over the years. In fact, these only enhanced my watching of it. Another Best Picture nominee that, outside of the dated manner of speaking, had a punchy dialogue that made you follow the story **and** the actors in focus, which is unsurprising for the radio star behind the infamous radio adaptation of "The War of the Worlds," and warranted and rewarded, actively watching it. It even gave you the first ever jump scare in film history just to keep you awake and watching.

• A Lightning round <sup>(er, bullet/s)</sup> of the other Best Picture nominees:
◦ Whiplash was anxiety-inducing in the most sensical way possible;
◦ Greta Gerwig's Little Women took an ensemble cast of big names and made you feel a sense of familiarity, filial longing, loss of innocence, heartbreak, and many more in each of these all-stars' moves, words, and camerawork. It felt earnest and not at all a "Hollywood adaption," so to speak;
◦I watched Dune right before watching Dune pt. 2, and it did great establishing the world-building for the core of pt. 2. haven't watched a genuine 2-parter movie since Back To The Future; (which was actually a 3-parter but parts 1 & 2 were still great on their own :D)
◦Good Will Hunting is a classic that just somehow escaped from me. Robin Williams is always great at underscoring humor before hitting you with a haymaker of a gut punch.

• Love Exposure is a stupid and crass movie that I cannot, with a good conscience, recommend to most people. It is weird, nonsensical, and a fever dream of a movie that lasted almost 4 hours long. If you Stephen Chow films, and think it's too weird for you, I would say this might not be for you. That being said, as a big Stephen Chow enjoyer, I had an absolute blast with every one-liner, visual joke, camerawork, visual effect and absurd plot point, which I don't think I could say for any other 4 hour movie. If you got here in this paragraph, I hope you do end up watching it <sup>on your own accord</sup> and liking it so that you can reach out and tell me about it. lol

• A couple of notable movies I watched in 2024 that were outside my conditions: Godzilla Minus One (rel. 2023 - ★★★★★) was a return to form to the best Gojira movies where the stories are about the humans living in Godzilla's vicinity, rather than a monster professional wrestling storyline that tries paint Godzilla as either a babyface(Good Guy) or a heel. (Bad Guy) Soundtrack and VFX were obviously great deserving of its awards and accolades; The Fall Guy(rel. 2024 - ★★★) was a good comedy with better action; everything else was just the "*Bacon*" <sup>(kek)</sup> It was an ode to stuntpeople in the industry by a long-time stuntperson in the industry, and it felt like it.

<sup>*Quick note/s: My rating system is in a /★★★★★ system, where average is ★★½. It does not represent whether I liked a movie or not, hence the "Liked?" column.</sup>

I ended up continuing this in 2025 at least, but they technically don't count in this context, so I reserve my review of those movies for personal conversations with people. [Say hi!](/#/contact)

Title: 2026: The Reading List Year
body:
In lieu of a list of New Year's resolutions in 2024, I started putting my money where my mouth is when it comes to my humble claims of being a film buff. I started a "[watchlist year](/#/other?uid=2024)" where I aimed to tick 12 movies off from my ever-growing watchlist. I ended up continuing this in 2025 and was planning to in 2026. However, my little sister ended up buying me a copy of James Clear's Atomic Habits in February on a whim. I offhandedly mention I've heard good things about it, while we're doing my seasonal pastime of perusing bookstores and imagining a reality where I was more of an avid reader of traditionally published written literature, rather than my usual readings of newspaper/news site/tech blog articles that are fighting for everyone's attention span with a Clickbait title or an obtuse amount of inline ads. (I understand these keep businesses afloat; it doesn't mean I can't be annoyed by it :P) As a kid, my mom and grandparents had a whole bookshelf of encyclopedias, with each letter having at least one book that made my young little arms shake as I tiptoe on a chair to reach whichever letter I'll be hyperfixating on that single day. I would just start reading at any page randomly, just absorbing little factoids about [insert letter here] things. There was no rhyme nor reason for my search for some knowledge. I was just amused by the little tickle my brain feels when I learn something I didn't even know I was unaware of. This chaotic knowledge gathering was later amplified and downright encouraged as my mom bought herself, and consequentially, me, a yearly almanac that would inform my sense of pop culture and the world around me. My dad, the computer programmer, would also install a little program in our house PC called "Britannica Online." This introduced my tiny brain to the concept of the computer being a device more than of a gaming console,(though my games were from the Jumpstart series) painting, and writing tool. It was home to many a-knowledge. and therefore the "brain-tickles" those come with. It even has videos and audios! I would cycle between reading my mom's almanacs, then search up the interesting tidbits/new words I encountered, in the digital encyclopedia... Speaking of digital encyclopedias: As many of us who needed to start needing to do research for our school papers, I was introduced to Wikipedia, a continuously growing library of information. It was around high school(7th-10th grade in the Philippines) that I developed a new hobby for the "brain-tickles" by doing a deep-dive into a specific topic, and using the hyperlinks across the Wikipedia article and dive deeper on those articles. I would iterate on this ad infinitum, or until I get stuck in an article I wasn't interested much by. Looking at you, [paint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paint). I would put up [Paint Drying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paint_Drying) but that's actually an interesting read. It was also around this time I was getting into manga, poetry collections, and per my peers' pressure, YA novels. Here, my new hobby introduced a quite niche bothersome problem. I was fairly interested in looking into IPs' world-building and lore, so most of the popular TV shows, movies, video games. AND books became quite unappealing to read because either I spoiled my appetite in learning about its world and story from reading, or I just had too high of an expectation for the execution of the lore I've read that it oftentimes end in disappointment. My tween brain did read and enjoy Rick Riordan's Percy Jackson series, Lian Tanner's "Museum of Thieves," and Michael Scott's Nicholas Flamel series. Unfortunately, as I got into college, plus moving across the globe, my reading has started to shift to being third in the queue, as my time between classes and/or on the commute prioritized a quicker dopamine hit to rest between the synchronous absorbing of knowledge in college + university. Here, video games, movies, and TV shows were just a more economic use of my perceived time. Hence, my current reading habits and desire. Being gifted a copy by my sis, as opposed to my own buying of the book, somehow compelled me to just start reading Atomic Habits in the corner of our living room. As I was reading through Clear's story in his introduction, he also introduced the idea of habits (both good and bad) being built, rather than what I initially thought were just inherent to someone's character. This tickled the brain, so I wanted to learn more. He laid out the reasonings behind the approach he's championing, clearly putting the foundation on the reader's brain that this is not just a book of productivity tricks and hacks, this is a philosophy book to change your way of thinking to build the systems that'll work for you, rather than a one-size-fits-all snake oil. It would be a disservice to even parrot any of Clear's laws without the surrounding context because the context is the reason it clicks. Earlier in my adult life, I tried Clear's app, printed out the laws to remind myself, and even listened to those that broke down the concepts on YouTube, but it did not stick until I actually sat down and read the context myself. There are 2 concepts I want to highlight by paraphrasing them how I understood them, which I'll leave to the end. In the meantime, I'll tell you that this book reignited my affinity towards reading, and I've aimed to make 2026 my reading list year, paralleling my 2024 watchlist year. Although I took all of February and some change with March just to finish my first book, so realistically speaking, I'm aiming to read 9 more books, hopefully more, but 9 is the goal. I wanted to make use of what worked in my watchlist year and improve upon it using what I learned from Atomic Habits. First was to make a list of the books I've been wanting to read, mostly with what I've gathered from my book-buying hobby, to **make it easy** to just continue reading after another:
Title Author Note Fiction Non-Fiction Technical Poetry Owned Library
Atomic Habits James Clear s/o to my sis.
7 habits of Highly Effective People Stephen R. Covey
The Truth Terry Pratchett
Small Gods Terry Pratchett
The Only Worlds We Know Michael Lee
Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code Martin Fowler
Out Natsuo Kirino RF Kuang was reading this at the time of her webinar
Taipei Story RF Kuang New RF Kuang book this year
The 6 Phase Meditation Method Vishen Lakhiani s/o to my auntie A.
Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Robert C. Martin
System Design Interview Alex Xu ByteByteGo's book/s
Murakami T Haruki Murakami s/o to my friend, Jonathan, for the gift.
Poetry Will Save Your Life Jill Bialosky Read only a quarter of it when I bought it initially. My schedule's fault; book was great.
The Craft of Scientific Presentations Michael Alley
A Rhetoric of Motives Kenneth Burke
The Pragmatic Programmer David Thomas, Andrew Hunt
Next, I'd need to **Make it obvious**. With my current reading, I claimed a chair in a corner of our living room my de facto reading nook, and at whatever point I stop reading, I would put my bookmark and place it on the coffee table beside it. This made it so that every time I walk past it by chance, I feel compelled to just "do a quick read." This also **made it easy** to just pick up my book and read. Another thing that worked in 2024 was that I started a spreadsheet of all the movies I've watched. It made it attractive, easy, and satisfying to actually sit down and give up my next couple of hours to a movie. It also helped with my mindful consumption of the film, being aware of what I liked, didn't like, and just how the movie made me feel or a lack of thereof. Writing my own thoughts and put into words the ideas in my head made the experience quite enjoyable, though there are still films that I have nothing to say about, but a spreadsheet isn't really a fun nor compelling way to track my progress and thoughts. I learned about letterboxd in 2025 and started to **make it attractive** to write my opinions on that, then. My only hang up is it being a social media platform where my thoughts felt so vulnerable that I would avoid writing my thoughts about my opinions on a movie more often. So, to **make it** *more* **attractive***, I wanted a way to have a similar platform like letterboxd or Goodreads but only is local to my device. Enter Mateusz Bąk's [OpenReads](openreads.app). Not only is it a lightweight open-source app that has all the things I needed, it also is written in Flutter so I enjoyed reading through his code (with the amount of open-source issues lately, this is just best practice before downloading to any device of yours) and finding out how it worked behind the scenes. Lastly, I wanted to challenge myself and expand my horizons. As you can tell with the books I've listed above, I mainly read nonfiction, while most of my friends read fiction. So to ensure I step out of my bubble, I promised my friends who like RF Kuang, I'd read her latest book when it comes out at the same time as him and have discussions like an informal book club. Also, I struck some book swap deals, where I would lend out a book to my friends from my library, while I get one from theirs. --- ## Key takeaways from Atomic Habits by Francis from Atomic Habits My paraphrased learnings from the book > Every action you take is a vote to becoming the person you'd like to be. > Missing once is a mistake; missing twice is a start of a habit. - "One step forward; two steps back" haunted me when I was younger. I would beat myself up every time I trip up on the way to becoming who I wanted to be. But looking back, I actually did more steps forward than steps back. I just took that saying from the ether and thought of it as fact. These two lessons from Clear put into perspective that each and every moment is an opportunity to become who I want to be. I should just keep picking the right direction ==as much as I can==. > The most effective way to change your habits is to focus not on *what* you want to achieve, but rather **who** you wish to become. - This particular one gave a perspective that I don't necessarily want to just tick off a checklist of things to do, and rather become the type of person that does those things, in this case, a reader. And ~7 months in and 6 books deep, I'd say I'm pretty much on the way there. Hope you achieve those goals too. Thanks for reading.
footnote:
I most likely won't share my thoughts similar to this for about most of what I read this year, aside from maybe a 'post-2026 post' but if I had thoughts I wanted to share here, why not? lol.
